analysis.one_liner: Bars states from taxing out-of-state businesses unless they have a physical presence there.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in 2007 by Sen. Chuck Schumer with a Republican cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a single hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded a 1959 federal law that limits how states tax businesses operating across state lines. It would have extended those protections beyond corporate income taxes to nearly all state business activity taxes, covered sales of services and intangible property as well as goods, and flatly prohibited any state from taxing a company that has no physical presence there. In short, a company could sell into a state, serve customers there, and gather information there without owing that state any business taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Large multistate companies — online and catalog retailers, service providers, financial firms — that sell into states where they have no office, employee, or property. They would owe no business activity taxes in those states, and the bill would also shield independent contractors and affiliate sellers whose work for them could otherwise create a taxable presence. In-state businesses would also be spared the cost of tracking and filing in many states' business tax regimes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Multistate retailers and out-of-state service firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the protections of the 1959 federal law (Public Law 86-272), which currently shield companies from state net income taxes on sales of tangible goods, to sales and transactions involving services, intangible property, and other non-goods transactions [S2][S3].

It prohibits any state from imposing a net income or other business activity tax on a company unless the company has a physical presence in that state — an employee, an exclusive agent, or property located there — with presence under 15 days a year excluded [S3].

It would apply these protections to all state and local business activity taxes, not just net income taxes, effective for taxable periods beginning January 1, 2008, while carving out sales and use taxes [S3].
It declares that use of independent contractors to solicit orders, make sales, or furnish information in a state does not by itself create a taxable presence there [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which would lose tax revenue they currently collect from out-of-state companies selling into their states; their residents, who would eventually pay the difference through other taxes or receive fewer services; and in-state businesses, which would keep paying state business taxes that their out-of-state competitors escape.

drawbacks.text: States would lose revenue from companies that sell into them without maintaining a physical presence; that revenue funds schools, roads, and other services residents use, so the cost would fall back on state budgets and taxpayers [S2][S3].

Local businesses with stores, offices, and employees in a state would continue paying that state's business taxes while out-of-state competitors selling the same goods and services into the state would not, putting them at a price disadvantage [S3].

The bill contained no small-business exception: a company of any size selling services or intangibles into a state would be exempt from that state's business activity taxes as long as it had no physical presence there [S3].

A good-faith argument for the bill is that multistate tax compliance is genuinely burdensome — businesses must track thousands of state and local tax rules — and a bright-line physical presence test is simple to administer; supporters would say states can still collect sales and use taxes, which the bill excludes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does address a real problem — the patchwork of state business tax rules is costly and confusing, and the 1959 law is outdated for a services and internet economy. But its remedy is one-sided: it hands tax relief to out-of-state sellers of all sizes without any offset for the states, and it does so at the expense of local businesses that remain fully taxable. A design that paired the bright-line rule with a small-business threshold or revenue backstop to states would have balanced the interests; this version did not.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 28, 2007 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Schumer introduced the bill on June 28, 2007, with Sen. Mike Crapo joining as its Republican cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S4][S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee or floor vote appears in the bill's complete action history for the remainder of the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill expired on January 3, 2009, when the 110th Congress ended, leaving existing state taxing authority and the 1959 federal framework unchanged [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments kept their authority to tax out-of-state companies that sell into their states, and in-store, in-state businesses faced no new untaxed competition from rivals beyond their borders.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State tax collectors and local businesses

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke on it upon introduction; it was then referred to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Joined Schumer in introducing the bill, making it bipartisan from the start.

for.name: National Conference of State Legislatures and other state and local government groups
for.role: Coalition representing state legislatures and local governments
for.what_they_did: Opposed expansion of the federal ban on state business-activity taxation in this era, arguing it strips state revenue.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership (Chair Max Baucus)
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; its only recorded action in the entire Congress was receiving the referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican cosponsor, but no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of the chamber's support or opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Multistate retailers, e-commerce and out-of-state service firms
industries.note: The bill would let them sell services, intangibles, and goods into states where they have no employees or property without owing any state business activity taxes there. States would have to shift the burden to residents or cut services, and local competitors would remain fully taxed.

The bill would forbid taxing out-of-state companies without physical presence and extend that ban to nearly all business activity taxes, shrinking state and local tax bases. Lost revenue means residents pay more elsewhere or receive fewer services.

industries.industry: Local and in-state businesses (brick-and-mortar retailers and service firms)
industries.note: Businesses with stores, offices, and staff in a state keep paying that state's business taxes while out-of-state rivals selling into the same market would be exempt. That tilts competition toward companies that avoid the state's tax system.

industries.industry: Affiliate marketers and independent sales contractors
industries.note: The bill would guarantee that working as an independent contractor or affiliate for an out-of-state company does not create a taxable presence for that company, protecting these income arrangements. Some of these are ordinary people earning side income, so their gain tracks the public's in part.
